hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">A quick introduction to the Microscaling (MX) data formats</a></li><li><a href="#1-tensor-memory-and-cuda-cores-kill-the-dequantization-vibe" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">1. Tensor memory and CUDA cores kill the dequantization vibe</a></li><li><a href="#2-death-by-a-thousand-quantizations" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">2. Death by a thousand quantizations</a></li><li><a href="#choosing-the-right-low-precision-recipe" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">Choosing the right low-precision recipe</a></li><li><a href="#embracing-tcgen05-mxfp8-block-scaled-matrix-multiplication" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">Embracing tcgen05 MXFP8 block-scaled matrix multiplication</a></li><li><a href="#expanding-to-mxfp8-grouped-matrix-multiplications" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">Expanding to MXFP8 grouped matrix multiplications</a></li></ul><ul><li><a href="#kernel-abstraction" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block pl-g1.5">Kernel abstraction</a></li><li><a href="#l2-cache-optimization-via-expert-wise-supergrouping" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block pl-g1.5">L2 cache optimization via expert-wise supergrouping</a></li><li><a href="#grouped-matrix-multiplication-benchmarks" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block pl-g1.5">Grouped matrix multiplication benchmarks</a></li><li><a href="#building-the-fastest-mxfp8-quantization-kernel-ever" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">Building the fastest MXFP8 quantization kernel ever</a></li><li><a href="#speedups" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">Speedups!</a></li><li><a href="#closing-thoughts" class="py-v1/12 hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">Closing thoughts</a></li></ul></div></div></nav><div class="prose prose--block prose--blog col-span-full!"><p>We want to build the world’s best AI coding models, but training large language models can be expensive. For instance, our largest internal models can take weeks to train on tens of thousands of GPUs. This is not only computationally expensive, but it also slows the pace at which improvements reach our users.</p>
<p>We recently began upgrading from Hopper GPUs (H100s) to Blackwell GPUs (B200s) and saw this as an opportunity to deeply optimize our training workloads. Profiling revealed that the main bottleneck was the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer, implemented with <a href="https://github.com/databricks/megablocks" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">MegaBlocks</a>, which accounted for nearly 53% of forward-pass time and 27% of backward-pass time.</p>
<p>That’s why, over the past few weeks, <strong>we rewrote the entire MoE layer from scratch at the GPU kernel level</strong> with zero dependencies on any CUDA libraries. Instead, we used pure, good old CUDA and PTX, with a few bits of <a href="https://github.com/HazyResearch/ThunderKittens" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">ThunderKittens</a> sprinkled in. As a result, we achieved a <strong>3.5x improvement in MoE layer performance for both the forward and backward passes</strong>, translating to a 1.5x end-to-end training speedup on Blackwell and a 2x speedup compared to our original Hopper setup. We believe our stack is faster than any combination of open-source alternatives available today.</p>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="Figure 1. Relative speedups of MXFP8 MoE compared to BF16 (normalized to 1.0)." loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-0.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-0.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-0.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div><figcaption>Figure 1. Relative speedups of MXFP8 MoE compared to BF16 (normalized to 1.0).</figcaption></figure>
<p>Most of this improvement came from transitioning from BF16 to <a href="https://www.opencompute.org/documents/ocp-microscaling-formats-mx-v1-0-spec-final-pdf" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">MXFP8</a> which we achieved with nearly zero loss in training quality. But this also taught us that going low precision is easier said than done. If not done carefully, MXFP8 training may offer minimal performance improvement over BF16 due to various kernel overheads. The MXFP8 training recipe is also not widely shared, meaning you have to discover the right approach yourself.</p>
<p>The following is our recipe, and a look at the ML work we do at Cursor.</p>
<h2 id="a-quick-introduction-to-the-microscaling-mx-data-formats" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#a-quick-introduction-to-the-microscaling-mx-data-formats" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>A quick introduction to the Microscaling (MX) data formats</h2>
<p>A common way to reduce the computational cost of large deep learning models is to use lower-precision activations and weights. However, converting them to narrow bit-width formats (e.g., 8 or fewer bits) introduces unacceptable rounding error unless the values are scaled appropriately. For example, some weights in a large model might be 0.0001, 0.0005, or –0.0007, but naively converting these to FP8 would round them all to the same number: zero, since the smallest positive value representable in FP8E4M3 is around 0.0019.</p>
<p>To address this, it is common to apply a per-tensor scaling factor, which rescales the tensor while keeping its values within the representable range of the target data format. This ensures that the available dynamic range is fully utilized. For example, if a tensor’s values are all between –0.0001 and 0.0001, its scaling factor could be set to 4,480,000. This would cause the tensor’s values after scaling to be in the range [–448, 448], which corresponds to the representable bounds of FP8E4M3.</p>
<p>Microscaling goes a step further by applying scaling to fine-grained sub-blocks of a tensor, rather than using a single scale factor for the entire tensor. The <strong>Microscaling (MX) format</strong> standardizes this approach by defining a set of low-precision, micro-scaled data formats. Full details are provided in its <a href="https://www.opencompute.org/documents/ocp-microscaling-formats-mx-v1-0-spec-final-pdf" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">specification</a>, which defines the following concrete MX-compliant formats:</p>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="Table 1. Concrete MX-compliant formats." loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-1.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-1.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-1.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div><figcaption>Table 1. Concrete MX-compliant formats.</figcaption></figure>
<p>For example, if we use the MXFP8 format with the E4M3 element type, the data would consist of FP8E4M3 elements with an FP8E8M0 scale factor applied to every consecutive 32-element block, as illustrated in the figure below.</p>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="Figure 2. MXFP8 quantization example: Each 1x32 block shares a scale." loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-2.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-2.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-2.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div><figcaption>Figure 2. MXFP8 quantization example: Each 1x32 block shares a scale.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Although microscaling can unlock significant performance gains, applying it in practice introduces several challenges and depends heavily on the underlying hardware. Let’s first look at why applying microscaling on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs can be particularly challenging.</p>
<h2 id="1-tensor-memory-and-cuda-cores-kill-the-dequantization-vibe" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#1-tensor-memory-and-cuda-cores-kill-the-dequantization-vibe" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>1. Tensor memory and CUDA cores kill the dequantization vibe</h2>
<p>In microscaled FP8 matrix multiplication, the computation is broken into smaller block-sized steps along the reduction dimension. After each blocked matrix multiplication, the partial result is <strong>dequantized</strong> using scale factors and then accumulated before proceeding to the next block.</p>
<p>For example, in the well-known <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">DeepSeek V3 (DSV3)</a> technical report, the A matrix was scaled in blocks of size <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7278em;vertical-align:-0.0833em"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">128</span></span></span></span> and the B matrix was scaled in blocks of size <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7278em;vertical-align:-0.0833em"></span><span class="mord">128</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">128</span></span></span></span>. This means the procedure is as follows:</p>
<ol>
<li>Perform a 128-block matrix multiplication:</li>
</ol>
<div class="prose-code-block"><pre class="shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark" style="background-color:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e;color:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8" tabindex="0"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">C_block </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> A[:, k</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">*</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF">128</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">:(k</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">+</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF">1</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">)</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">*</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF">128</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">] </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">@</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> B[k</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">*</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF">128</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">:(k</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">+</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF">1</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">)</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">*</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF">128</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">, :]</span></span></code></pre></div>
<ol>
<li>Apply dequantization using scale factors:</li>
</ol>
<div class="prose-code-block"><pre class="shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark" style="background-color:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e;color:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8" tabindex="0"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">C_block </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> A_scale[:, k] </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">*</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> C_block </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">*</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> B_scale[k, :]</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>where <code>A_scale</code> is broadcast across 128 elements along the K dimension and <code>B_scale</code> is broadcast across 128 elements along both dimensions</p>
<ol>
<li>Accumulate the dequantized block:</li>
</ol>
<div class="prose-code-block"><pre class="shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark" style="background-color:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e;color:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8" tabindex="0"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">C </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">+=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> C_block</span></span></code></pre></div>
<ol>
<li>Proceed to the next block along the reduction dimension:</li>
</ol>
<div class="prose-code-block"><pre class="shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark" style="background-color:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e;color:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8" tabindex="0"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">k </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">+=</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF"> 1</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>This method naturally works well on the Hopper architecture (on which DSV3 was trained), because (1) the results of the tensor core matrix multiplies (via <code>wgmma</code> instruction) are accumulated in registers, and (2) you can pipeline matrix multiplies, asynchronously launching other tensor core matrix multiplies while performing dequantization with CUDA cores. Because everything is accumulated in the registers, no additional data movement is required between the matrix multiplies.</p>
<p>This is no longer the case on Blackwell GPUs due to <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#tensor-memory" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">tensor memory</a> (TMEM). TMEM is a new set of on-chip, SM-local memory added on Blackwell GPUs. Unlike Hopper GPUs, where the results of tensor core matrix multiplies accumulate directly in registers, Blackwell GPUs accumulate them in TMEM (via <code>tcgen05.mma</code> instruction). To perform custom arithmetic on the accumulators, you must transfer the results from TMEM to registers, process them with CUDA cores, write them back to TMEM, and then wait for all of these instructions to complete because the data movements are asynchronous. Although TMEM is faster to access than shared memory (SMEM), this still kills tensor core occupancy.</p>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="Figure 3. Gantt chart taken from our custom Blackwell attention kernel. First row shows the tensor core activity (QKᵀ). Second row shows the CUDA core activity (TMEM → registers, then softmax). TMEM → register latency causes the tensor core pipeline bubble." loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-3.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-3.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-3.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div><figcaption>Figure 3. Gantt chart taken from our custom Blackwell attention kernel. First row shows the tensor core activity (QKᵀ). Second row shows the CUDA core activity (TMEM → registers, then softmax). TMEM → register latency causes the tensor core pipeline bubble.</figcaption></figure>
<p>At first glance, this suggests a pipelined approach: divide the TMEM into chunks and run matrix multiplies on one chunk while data movement and dequantization are happening on the other chunk.</p>
<p>But there’s another problem here: while the Blackwell tensor cores doubled in TFLOP/s compared to Hopper, the FP32 CUDA cores only improved by about 33% (60 → 80 TFLOP/s). With 32-block scaling, the amount of computation spent on dequantization is 1/32 the matrix multiply (both involve multiplication and addition; with CUDA core dequantization you have to manually accumulate), but the speed of dequantization is 1/56 the matrix multiply (4,500 TFLOP/s theoretical). As a result, dequantization on CUDA cores can take nearly 1.76x the time spent on matrix multiplication. This is horrible.</p>

class="pb-v5/12 pr-g1 border-theme-border-02 border-b text-left text-sm font-bold whitespace-pre [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0">Hopper (H100 SXM5)</th><th class="pb-v5/12 pr-g1 border-theme-border-02 border-b text-left text-sm font-bold whitespace-pre [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0">Blackwell (B200)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr class="border-theme-border-02 border-b last:border-b-0"><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">FP8 Tensor Core Throughput</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm TFLOP/s</td></tr><tr class="border-theme-border-02 border-b last:border-b-0"><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">FP32 CUDA Core Throughput</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">60 TFLOP/s</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">80 TFLOP/s</td></tr><tr class="border-theme-border-02 border-b last:border-b-0"><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 ">1.76x</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="mt-v1 text-theme-text-sec text-sm">Table 2. Relative Dequantization Cost on Hopper vs Blackwell.</p></div>
<p>Empirically, we could not even surpass Hopper’s realistic FP8 throughput of 1,500 TFLOP/s with any variation of the above approach. And this isn’t even considering the <em>quantization</em> overhead.</p>
<h2 id="2-death-by-a-thousand-quantizations" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#2-death-by-a-thousand-quantizations" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>2. Death by a thousand quantizations</h2>
<p>Every matrix has to be FP8-quantized before getting fed to a FP8 matrix multiplication kernel. It’s essential to reduce and hide the quantization time as much as possible. When not handled carefully, quantization kernels can overtake the GPU time.</p>
<p>To understand how dominant quantization can be, let’s consider a simple matrix multiplication <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.07153em">C</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7667em;vertical-align:-0.0833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05017em">B</span></span></span></span>, where:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span></span></span></span> is <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7667em;vertical-align:-0.0833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">M</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.07153em">K</span></span></span></span></p>
</li>
<li>
<p><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05017em">B</span></span></span></span> is <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7667em;vertical-align:-0.0833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.07153em">K</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span></span></span></span></p>
</li>
<li>
<p><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.07153em">C</span></span></span></span> is <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7667em;vertical-align:-0.0833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">M</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span></span></span></span></p>
</li>
</ul>
<p>In grouped matrix multiplications for MoE training, it’s common for <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">M</span></span></span></span> to be very large compared to <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.07153em">K</span></span></span></span> and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span></span></span></span>. So let’s take:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">M</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8389em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord">131</span><span class="mord"><span class="mpunct">,</span></span><span class="mord">072</span></span></span></span></p>
</li>
<li>
<p><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.07153em">K</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8389em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord">7</span><span class="mord"><span class="mpunct">,</span></span><span class="mord">168</span></span></span></span></p>
</li>
<li>
<p><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8389em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mord"><span class="mpunct">,</span></span><span class="mord">048</span></span></span></span></p>
</li>
</ul>
<p>With this, the total number of floating point operations needed for the matrix multiplication itself is:</p>
<span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8389em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord">131</span><span class="mord"><span class="mpunct">,</span></span><span class="mord">072</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7278em;vertical-align:-0.0833em"></span><span class="mord">7168</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7278em;vertical-align:-0.0833em"></span><span class="mord">2048</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord">FLOP</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord">3.85</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord">TFLOP</span></span></span></span></span></span>
<p>Our benchmarks show that Blackwell GPUs (B200s) have an FP8 matrix multiplication throughput of ~3,300 TFLOP/s. This means the expected wall-clock time to execute the matrix multiplication is:</p>
<span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">3.85</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> TFLOP </span></span><span class="mord">/</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> </span></span><span class="mord">3</span><span class="mord"><span class="mpunct">,</span></span><span class="mord">300</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> TFLOP/s</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1.16</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> ms</span></span></span></span></span></span>
<p>However, we also need to consider the time to quantize the A and B matrices. Since quantization is memory bandwidth-bound, the key factor is the total data movement. Let’s assume the original matrices are in BF16 (2 bytes) and the scale block size is 32. This means we must:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p>Load A: <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8389em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord">131</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">072</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8389em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord">7</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">168</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord">B</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord">1.88</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> GB</span></span></span></span></span></p>
</li>
<li>

<p>In total, this is approximately 2.9 GB worth of High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) reads and writes. Assuming a sustainable HBM throughput of 6.5 TB/s on B200s, an optimized FP8 quantization kernel would take:</p>
<span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">2.9</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> GB </span></span><span class="mord">/</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> </span></span><span class="mord">6.5</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> TB/s</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">≈</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">0.44</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> ms</span></span></span></span></span></span>
<p>That’s almost 40% of the matrix multiplication time. In a common scenario where we also transpose-quantize the A matrix for backward propagation, this doubles to 0.88 ms, <strong>about 76% of the matrix multiplication time</strong>!</p>
<p>Even though FP8 matrix multiplication is theoretically 2x faster than BF16 matrix multiplication, quantization time can truly kill the performance gain. The above analysis is also <em>optimistic</em> because it assumes a block-scaled FP8 matrix multiplication running at 3,300 TFLOP/s, which is much higher than what is typically achieved in end-to-end MoE training. In the worst case, the quantization could take longer than the FP8 matrix multiplication, thus making the overall FP8 computation slower than BF16.</p>
<p>There do exist some fast, open-source FP8 quantization kernels, namely from NVIDIA <a href="https://github.com/NVIDIA/TransformerEngine/blob/dd083bdfca296294322f2b5f8143ce54ee15db22/transformer_engine/common/util/cast_kernels.cuh#L1005" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">TransformerEngine</a> or Pytorch <a href="https://github.com/pytorch/ao/blob/main/torchao/csrc/cuda/mx_kernels/mxfp8_quantize.cuh" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">TorchAO</a>. However, our microbenchmarks have shown that they leave bandwidth on the table, running at around 4.5 TB/s. Purely relying on intra-SM instructions (e.g., <code>cp.async.bulk</code>), we know that Blackwell can easily run at 6~7 TB/s HBM bandwidth.</p>
<p>Furthermore, NVIDIA’s MXFP8 <code>tcgen05.mma</code> instruction, the PTX instruction for tensor core matrix multiplication, requires <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#tcgen05-mma-scale-factor-a-layout-1x" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">a slightly unintuitive</a> <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#tcgen05-mma-scale-factor-b" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">scale factor layout</a>. With 32-block scaling, TransformerEngine or TorchAO quantization kernels return the scale factor in a naive M x N / 32 layout. This must then be reshaped, either in PyTorch or by fusing the reshaping logic into other kernels, both of which negatively affect performance. In practice, you really don’t want to process scale factors inside the matrix multiply kernels. The fastest way to load them is by taking the HBM → SMEM (<code>cp.async.bulk</code>) path and then the SMEM → TMEM (<code>tcgen05.cp</code>) path; the moment a scale detours through the register tile, the tensor vibe is dead.</p>
<p>Next, we explain how we addressed the aforementioned challenges, starting with our approach to quantization.</p>
<h2 id="choosing-the-right-low-precision-recipe" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#choosing-the-right-low-precision-recipe" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Choosing the right low-precision recipe</h2>
<p>To match the training quality of BF16, we ran a series of low-precision experiments, measuring how much each recipe diverged from BF16. From these, we identified the one that yields training loss convergence nearly identical to that of BF16 for our workloads.</p>
<p>Specifically, we use the MXFP8 format with FP8E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) as the element data type, FPE8M0 (8 exponent bits) as the scale data type, and a scaling block size of 32. We also adopt the MXFP8 quantization recipe from the paper, “<a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.08027" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Recipes for Pre-training LLMs with MXFP8</a>”. Let:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p>BF16 (or FP32) vector <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.22222em">V</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">{</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.22222em">V</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3117em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.2222em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">∣</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6595em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">i</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="minner">…</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">31</span><span class="mclose">}</span></span></span></span></p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Corresponding FP8E4M3 vector <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8778em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">{</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3117em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:0em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">∣</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6595em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">i</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="minner">…</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">31</span><span class="mclose">}</span></span></span></span></p>
</li>
<li>
<p>FP8E8M0 scale S</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p>We calculate Q and S as follows:</p>
<span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05764em">S</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1.2em;vertical-align:-0.35em"></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord text"><span class="mord texttt">cast_to_fp8e8m0</span></span></span><span class="mord"><span class="delimsizing size1">(</span></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord text"><span class="mord texttt">absolute_max</span></span></span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.22222em">V</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mord">/448</span><span class="mord"><span class="delimsizing size1">)</span></span></span></span></span></span>
<span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8778em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3117em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:0em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1.2em;vertical-align:-0.35em"></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord text"><span class="mord texttt">cast_to_fp8e4m3</span></span></span><span class="mord"><span class="delimsizing size1">(</span></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.22222em">V</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3117em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.2222em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mord">/</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05764em">S</span><span class="mord"><span class="delimsizing size1">)</span></span></span></span></span></span>
<p>where <code>cast_to_fp8e8m0</code> rounds <strong>up</strong> to the nearest powers of 2 and min-clamps to <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8141em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">2</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8141em"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mtight">−</span><span class="mord mtight">127</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, and <code>cast_to_fp8e4m3</code> saturates out-of-range values and rounds to nearest, ties to even.</p>
<p>With this, our FP8 training loss matched the BF16 training loss:</p>

BF16 vs MXFP8 Training Loss over 10k steps: nearly indistinguishable." loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-4.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-4.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-4.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div><figcaption>Figure 4. BF16 vs MXFP8 Training Loss (9k–10k steps) with a specific data point at step 9832.</figcaption></figure>
<h2 id="embracing-tcgen05-mxfp8-block-scaled-matrix-multiplication" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#embracing-tcgen05-mxfp8-block-scaled-matrix-multiplication" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Embracing tcgen05 MXFP8 block-scaled matrix multiplication</h2>
<p>On the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, MX formats are baked into the tensor cores. Block scaling is invoked through the <code>tcgen05.mma...block_scale</code> instruction and handled in hardware. This eliminates the need to move data out of TMEM for dequantization, since everything occurs during the tensor core matrix multiplication. Our MXFP8 matrix multiplication kernel design must therefore revolve around <code>tcgen05.mma</code> and operate <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#tcgen05-kind-shapes" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">within</a> <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#tcgen05-block-scaling" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">its</a> <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#tcgen05-mma-instructions-mma" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">constraints</a> to achieve maximum performance.</p>
<p>There are several important considerations. First, the <code>tcgen05.mma</code> instruction requires only a single thread to launch asynchronously. This contrasts with Hopper, where the <code>wgmma</code> instruction needs an entire warpgroup (128 threads) to launch asynchronously. Consequently, we have to deviate from the producer-consumer pattern common in Hopper kernels, where 256+ threads are dedicated to launching matrix multiplications.</p>
<p>Second, <code>tcgen05.mma</code> supports 2-CTA matrix multiplication, where two SMs collaboratively execute a matrix multiplication by sharing the B matrix. This reduces both memory traffic and shared memory usage, allowing for a deeper matrix multiplication pipeline. Our benchmarks indicate that this 2-CTA mode delivers about a 15~20% speedup for MXFP8 matrix multiplications compared to non-clustered versions, making it essential for peak performance.</p>
<p>Third, as noted earlier, <code>tcgen05.mma</code> accumulates results in TMEM rather than in registers. While this reduces register pressure, it also introduces additional data movement between TMEM and registers through the <code>tcgen05.ld</code> and <code>tcgen05.st</code> instructions. We must ensure that these data movements are minimized.</p>
<p>Finally, <code>tcgen05.mma</code> instruction requires the scale factor to reside in TMEM. However, there is no direct method to load the scales from HBM into TMEM. The fastest approach is to first load the data from HBM into on-chip SMEM using the <code>cp.async.bulk.tensor</code> instruction (leveraging the Tensor Memory Accelerator, or TMA), and then transfer it from SMEM to TMEM using the <code>tcgen05.cp</code> instruction. For this to work, scale factors must be stored in the layout expected by <code>tcgen05.mma</code>, as explained later in this post.</p>
<p>All of the instructions involved in these considerations — <code>tcgen05.mma</code>, <code>cp.async.bulk.tensor</code>, <code>tcgen05.cp</code>, <code>tcgen05.ld</code>, and <code>tcgen05.st</code> — are launched asynchronously by a single thread. This allows us to apply warp specialization and design a pipelined dataflow, using TMEM and SMEM as circular buffers.</p>
<p>To do this, we first partition TMEM and SMEM. On Blackwell, we are given 128x512 TMEM (32-bit per cell) and 227 KB of contiguous SMEM per threadblock. We divide TMEM into 5 slots for A and B scale storage, leaving space for matrix multiplication accumulations (MMA). Similarly, in SMEM we reserve space for storing MMA results back to HBM, and partition the rest into 5 slots for loading input tiles and scale factors. The layout is illustrated below.</p>

Simplified SMEM allocation: 5 slots reserved for input tiles and scales</figcaption></figure>
<p>With this setup, we design a pipeline where certain warps continuously load input tiles and scale from HBM to SMEM, others move scales from SMEM to TMEM, others launch the MMAs, and some occasionally load the TMEM accumulator into registers, store it in SMEM, and TMA-store it back to HBM.</p>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="Figure 8. Simplified MXFP8 Matrix Multiplication Pipeline" loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-8.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-8.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fkernels-8.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div><figcaption>Figure 8. Simplified MXFP8 Matrix Multiplication Pipeline</figcaption></figure>
<p>Specifically, we assign 3 warpgroups (384 threads) to each threadblock, and specialize the warpgroups into two: 2 warpgroups will only perform TMEM → register → SMEM → HBM data flow, which has the highest register pressure. The other warpgroup will do warp-specialization. Warp 0 loads the input tiles from HBM to SMEM, warp 1 loads the scale from HBM to SMEM, warp 2 loads the scale from SMEM to TMEM, and warp 3 launches the tensor core matrix multiplies. We also implement a <strong>persistent grid pattern</strong>, assigning a single threadblock per SM (148 on Blackwell GPUs) so that new input tiles can be loaded while results are being stored back to HBM.</p>
<p>The pseudo-code for the pipeline looks as follows:</p>

<p>One unavoidable limitation in block-scaled matrix multiplication on Blackwell GPUs is the size of TMEM. Our microbenchmarks show that Blackwell tensor cores achieve the highest throughput when the full 128x512 TMEM is used as the accumulator. For 2-CTA FP8 matrix multiplication, this corresponds to consistently running two 256x32x256 <code>tcgen05.mma</code> instructions. Each <code>tcgen05.mma</code> consumes a 128x256 region of TMEM per CTA, so two of them together fully occupy the 128x512 TMEM arrays across both CTAs.</p>
<p>When scale factors must also reside in TMEM, however, we can only execute a single 256x32x256 <code>tcgen05.mma</code> instruction at a time using just a 128x256 region of TMEM. As a result, performance degradation is unavoidable. For example, the throughput of a 16,384x16,384x16,384 FP8 matrix multiplication drops from 3,200 TFLOP/s to 3,040 TFLOP/s under this constraint.</p>
<p>These throughput numbers apply only to pure FP8 matrix multiplication. With MXFP8 block scaling, throughput inevitably decreases further due to TMEM pipelining overhead. In practice, we achieve around 2,750 TFLOP/s with L2 cache clearance for block-scaled MXFP8 matrix multiplication kernels. Even so, this remains ~1.83x faster than standard BF16 matrix multiplication, which typically reaches 1,500~1,550 TFLOP/s on optimal shapes. Not too bad of a start!</p>
<h2 id="expanding-to-mxfp8-grouped-matrix-multiplications" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#expanding-to-mxfp8-grouped-matrix-multiplications" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Expanding to MXFP8 grouped matrix multiplications</h2>
<p>A standalone MXFP8 matrix multiplication kernel is a useful first step, but during MXFP8 MoE training, its applications are limited (e.g., shared expert scenarios). To fully support MoE in MXFP8, we need <em>grouped</em> matrix multiplication kernels, specifically:</p>
<ol>
<li>
<p>Grouped forward propagation (Fprop) / data gradient (Dgrad)</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Grouped weight gradient (Wgrad)</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>Note that these variants are part of the reason we are building these kernels from scratch. To date, we have not found any open-source alternative that fully supports MXFP8 MoE training with 32-block scaling.</p>
<p>At the kernel level, grouped Fprop and Dgrad share the same structure. The only difference is that Dgrad requires accumulation, since the input tensor passes through both the up and gate projections. But this can be easily implemented by replacing the <code>cp.async.bulk.tensor</code> instruction with <code>cp.reduce.async.bulk.tensor</code>, which can perform atomic add-store to HBM asynchronously.</p>
<p>Given the following matrices:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>A</strong>: <code>num_tokens</code> x <code>in_dim</code></p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>W</strong>: <code>E</code> x <code>in_dim</code> x <code>out_dim</code>, where <code>E</code> is the number of experts on the current rank</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>O</strong>: <code>num_tokens</code> x <code>out_dim</code></p>
</li>
</ul>
<p>and assuming tokens are ordered by expert index, the grouped Fprop/Dgrad kernel performs:</p>
<div class="prose-code-block"><pre class="shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark" style="background-color:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e;color:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8" tabindex="0"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">for</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> i </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">in</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF"> range</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">(num_routed_experts):</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    start </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF"> 0</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583"> if</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> i </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">==</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF"> 0</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583"> else</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> end</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    end </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> start </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">+</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> assigned_tokens_per_expert[i]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    O[start:end, :] </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> A[start:end, :] </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">@</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> W[i, :, :]</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Grouped Wgrad, on the other hand, differs in that expert division occurs along the K (reduction) axis rather than the M axis. It computes:</p>
<div class="prose-code-block"><pre class="shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark" style="background-color:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e;color:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8" tabindex="0"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">for</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> i </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">in</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF"> range</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">(num_routed_experts):</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    start </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF"> 0</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583"> if</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> i </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">==</span><span style="color:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF"> 0</span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583"> else</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> end</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    end </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> start </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">+</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> assigned_tokens_per_expert[i]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    W_grad[i, :, :] </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> A.T[:, start:end] </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">@</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> O[start:end, :]</span></span></code></pre></div>
<h3 id="kernel-abstraction" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#kernel-abstraction" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Kernel abstraction</h3>
<p>At the kernel level, the common unit of work is a matrix multiply-accumulate over a specified row, column, and reduction range. Abstracting this unit proved highly useful for implementing grouped matrix multiplication kernels and allowed us to reuse the original MXFP8 matrix multiplication kernel with minimal changes. Accordingly, we factored out the original kernel:</p>
<div class="prose-code-block"><pre class="shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark" style="background-color:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e;color:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8" tabindex="0"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#6A737D;--shiki-dark:#6A737D">// All units of 128</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">int</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> expert_idx </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> ...</span><span style="color:#6A737D;--shiki-dark:#6A737D"> // 0 for 2D case</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">int</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> row_block_idx </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> ...</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">int</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> col_block_idx </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> ...</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">int</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> reduction_block_start_idx </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> ...</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">int</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> reduction_block_end_idx </span><span style="color:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> ...</span></span>
<span class="line"></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#6A737D;--shiki-dark:#6A737D">// Based on MXFP8 matrix multiplication implemented above</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#6A737D;--shiki-dark:#6A737D">// Runs at 256x128 granularity when possible (if not, 128x128)</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0">run_mxfp8_matmul</span><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">(</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    expert_idx,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    row_block_idx, </span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    col_block_idx, </span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    reduction_block_start_idx, </span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    reduction_block_end_idx</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">);</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>With this abstraction, implementing the grouped MXFP8 matrix multiplication variants reduces to designing the appropriate loop structures and assigning indices correctly before launching the above abstraction. However, naive looping can significantly hurt performance due to poor L2 cache utilization.</p>
<h3 id="l2-cache-optimization-via-expert-wise-supergrouping" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#l2-cache-optimization-via-expert-wise-supergrouping" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>L2 cache optimization via expert-wise supergrouping</h3>
<p>Maintaining high L2 cache utilization is critical. In our benchmarks, inefficient HBM access patterns could reduce performance by nearly 50% in grouped matrix multiplication kernels. To address this, we applied <strong>supergrouping</strong>, <a href="https://github.com/HazyResearch/ThunderKittens/blob/6c27e28c8115d1839d9eeeb530913c184a75fc87/kernels/matmul/FP8/matmul.cu#L37" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">a heuristic from ThunderKittens kernels</a> that maximizes L2 reuse by ensuring that the region of the output matrix computed by all 148 SMs at any given time is as square as possible. You can learn more about this by reading the linked kernel code above.</p>
<p>A key enhancement for our grouped matrix multiplication kernels was applying supergrouping <em>per expert</em>, considering only the submatrix belonging to the current expert rather than the entire output matrix. This proved especially effective for grouped Wgrad, where the reduction axis is often narrow due to expert partitioning. A narrow reduction axis leads to lower tensor core utilization, making memory bandwidth the primary bottleneck.</p>
<p>With the right matrix multiplication kernel abstraction and expert-wise L2 cache optimization, we achieved ~2,650 TFLOP/s with grouped MXFP8 matrix multiplication kernels — only a 4% drop compared to the non-grouped version. Great!</p>
<h3 id="grouped-matrix-multiplication-benchmarks" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#grouped-matrix-multiplication-benchmarks" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Grouped matrix multiplication benchmarks</h3>
<p>The closest open-source alternative on Blackwell for grouped Fprop/Dgrad/Wgrad is DeepSeek’s DeepGEMM. DeepGEMM differs slightly in that it uses 1x128 and 128x128 scale blocks for the A and B matrices, which comes at the cost of reduced accuracy. Still, it is the only alternative available, so we integrated DeepGEMM into our internal model training and profiled its performance. While DeepGEMM excelled on certain input shapes in our microbenchmarks, our end-to-end benchmarks showed that our kernels outperformed it for our workloads.</p>
<div class="table-wrapper"><table class="w-full"><thead><tr><th class="pb-v5/12 pr-g1 border-theme-border-02 border-b text-left text-sm font-bold whitespace-pre [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0"></th><th class="pb-v5/12 pr-g1 border-theme-border-02 border-b text-left text-sm font-bold whitespace-pre [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0">DeepSeek DeepGEMM</th><th class="pb-v5/12 pr-g1 border-theme-border-02 border-b text-left text-sm font-bold whitespace-pre [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0">Ours</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr class="border-theme-border-02 border-b last:border-b-0"><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">Grouped Fprop / Dgrad</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">0.67 ms</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0 font-bold ">0.43 ms</td></tr><tr class="border-theme-border-02 border-b last:border-b-0"><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">Grouped Wgrad</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">0.71 ms</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0 font-bold ">0.65 ms</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="mt-v1 text-theme-text-sec text-sm">Table 3. Average latency for grouped Fprop/Dgrad and Wgrad kernels during internal model training.</p></div>
<p>It is also important to note that the above benchmarks <strong>exclude quantization time</strong>. DeepGEMM does not provide optimized quantization kernels, and without them, end-to-end performance can quickly degrade. In the worst case, it can even be slower than BF16 training.</p>
<h2 id="building-the-fastest-mxfp8-quantization-kernel-ever" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#building-the-fastest-mxfp8-quantization-kernel-ever" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Building the fastest MXFP8 quantization kernel ever</h2>
<p>As noted earlier, existing MXFP8 quantization kernels are not only suboptimal but also require reshaping to match <code>tcgen05.mma</code> scale factor layout, incurring extra runtime overhead. Our goal, therefore, was to design a quantization kernel that:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p>Fully saturates memory bandwidth, preferably exceeding 6 TB/s for large M-dimension shapes.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Produces the scale matrix <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#tcgen05-mma-scale-factor-a-layout-1x" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">in the exact layout</a> <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#tcgen05-mma-scale-factor-b-layout-1x" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">expected by</a> <code>tcgen05.mma</code>, allowing our MXFP8 kernel to execute HBM → SMEM → TMEM data flow without intermediate transformations.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p>It turned out there was no single “magic” design that instantly gave us peak performance; it was a combination of the right primitives and numerous micro-optimizations discovered through trial and error. The most significant wins came from removing TMA swizzling in favor of a manual swizzling pattern to reduce intra-warp overhead, relying on the warp scheduler and inter-threadblock asynchrony rather than manual intra-threadblock overlapping, and minimizing SMEM and register usage to increase SM occupancy. Then there are all the standard optimizations including the TMAs, eliminating SMEM bank conflicts, leveraging fast vector intrinsics, etc. But there really isn’t much to generalize.</p>
<p>With these optimizations, we implemented an MXFP8 quantization kernel that sustains 6.2+ TB/s while producing the scale matrix in a layout directly compatible with <code>tcgen05.mma</code>. To the best of our knowledge, this is the fastest MXFP8 quantization kernel available for MoE training.</p>
<div class="table-wrapper"><table class="w-full"><thead><tr><th class="pb-v5/12 pr-g1 border-theme-border-02 border-b text-left text-sm font-bold whitespace-pre [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0"></th><th class="pb-v5/12 pr-g1 border-theme-border-02 border-b text-left text-sm font-bold whitespace-pre [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0">NVIDIA TransformerEngine</th><th class="pb-v5/12 pr-g1 border-theme-border-02 border-b text-left text-sm font-bold whitespace-pre [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0">PyTorch TorchAO</th><th class="pb-v5/12 pr-g1 border-theme-border-02 border-b text-left text-sm font-bold whitespace-pre [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0">Ours</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr class="border-theme-border-02 border-b last:border-b-0"><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">Naive</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">5236.35 GB/s</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">5245.15 GB/s</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">Not applicable</td></tr><tr class="border-theme-border-02 border-b last:border-b-0"><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">With reshape</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">4430.27 GB/s</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0  ">4524.45 GB/s</td><td class="pt-v5/12 pr-g1 md:pt-v7/12 text-left align-top text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap [&amp;:last-of-type]:pr-0 font-bold ">6212.21 GB/s</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="mt-v1 text-theme-text-sec text-sm">Table 4. MXFP8 quantization kernel comparison (E4M3, 32-block scaling) by memory bandwidth utilization. &quot;With reshape&quot; includes the time to reshape the scale factor for tcgen05.mma.</p></div>
<p>Other optimizations to the MXFP8 quantization included building a fused quantization kernel that outputs both non-transposed and transposed results (the latter needed for backward passes), as well as fusing MXFP8 quantization logic directly into other kernels to minimize HBM access as much as possible. For example, we attached MXFP8 dequantization/quantization logic to the prologue and epilogue of our fused MXFP8 SwiGLU kernel.</p>
<h2 id="speedups" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#speedups" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Speedups!</h2>
<p>With all the optimizations described above, we achieved <strong>3.5x faster MoE layer execution for both the forward and backward passes while maintaining the same training quality</strong>. When tested on one of our internal models, this translated into a 1.5x end-to-end training speedup on Blackwell and a 2x speedup compared to our original Hopper setup, measured in tokens per second per GPU (TPS/GPU). We believe that our stack runs MXFP8 MoE training faster than any combination of open-source alternatives.</p>

Performance comparisons (internal model). Note: Blackwell BF16 MoE was a direct port of the Hopper code</p></div>
<h2 id="closing-thoughts" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#closing-thoughts" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Closing thoughts</h2>
<p>We still have plenty of work ahead and many kernels left to optimize. Our current efforts focus on building more efficient multi-GPU communication, improving custom attention kernels, and preparing to transition to <strong>FP4</strong> for future MoE training runs.</p>
<p>If you are interested in writing and optimizing high-performance kernels, training large coding models, or our work broadly, we’d love to hear from you. Reach out to us at <a href="mailto:hiring@cursor.com" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">hiring@cursor.com</a>.</p>
<p>Special thanks to Benjamin Spector, Sasha Rush, Less Wright, Federico Cassano, Rohan Shah, Jacob Jackson, Sujay Jayakar, and Shengtong Zhang for reading this post and offering valuable However, converting them to narrow bit-width formats (e.g., 8 or fewer bits) introduces unacceptable rounding error unless the values are scaled appropriately. For example, some weights in a large model might be 0.0001, 0.0005, or –0.0007, but naively converting these to FP8 would round them all to the same number: zero, since the smallest positive value representable in FP8E4M3 is around 0.0019.\"}]\n38:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"To address this, it is common to apply a per-tensor scaling factor, which rescales the tensor while keeping its values within the representable range of the target data format. This ensures that the available dynamic range is fully utilized. For example, if a tensor’s values are all between –0.0001 and 0.0001, its scaling factor could be set to 4,480,000. This would cause the tensor’s values after scaling to be in the range [–448, 448], which corresponds to the representable bounds of FP8E4M3.\"}]\n39:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"Microscaling goes a step further by applying scaling to fine-grained sub-blocks of a tensor, rather than using a single scale factor for the entire tensor.
